msIdentifier.msName: Codex Argenteus (so named by Bonaventura Vulcanius in 1597)
Fragmentum Spirense / Folium Spirense / Haffner folium (after its discoverer)

msContents.summary: The manuscript originally transmitted the four Gospels in the so-called "Western" order: the Gospel of Matthew, the Gospel of John, the Gospel of Luke, and the Gospel of Mark. The Speyer leaf preserves Mark 16:12–20. The presence of wormholes in this leaf suggests that it originally followed a wooden board, and therefore that it constituted the final leaf of the codex.
msContents.textLang: The language of the manuscript is Gothic

msItem.title: Gospel of Matthew
msItem.note: In Matthew, 76 leaves are missing and 22 survive (approximately 75% lost)

msItem.title: Gospel of John
msItem.note: In John, 29 leaves are missing and 45 survive (approximately 40% lost)

msItem.title: Gospel of Luke
msItem.note: In Luke, 36 leaves are missing and 70 survive (approximately 35% lost)

msItem.title: Gospel of Mark
msItem.note: In Mark, 7 leaves are missing and 50 survive in Uppsala (approximately 8% lost)

msItem.title: Gospel of Mark (Speyer's folio)
msItem.note: One further leaf—the final one—preserved in Speyer, containing Mark 16:12–20

support.material: Parchment, probably made from kid skin, extremely thin and prepared with exceptional care. Purple-coloured: for the dyeing—which varies from leaf to leaf and between hair and flesh sides—both orchil and indigo were probably used; visual analysis further suggests the combined use of orchil (outer areas) and folium (within the written area).
support.p: In 1998 the parchment underwent radiocarbon (C14) analysis, which indicated a date not later than 550.

extent.measure: The manuscript originally consisted of 336 leaves
187 leaves survive in Uppsala and 1 in Speyer (188 total surviving)
Ca. 6.5 per line (130 mm divided by 20 lines)

supportDesc.foliation: The leaves were numbered in pencil in the upper right margin after they had been disbound and rebound in the order of the Vulgate (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John), as already attested in the editio princeps (1665). This new pagination dates to the nineteenth century.

collation.p: The quires are mostly quaternions, except for the final quire of each Gospel. Of the original quires of the Codex Argenteus, 37 were quaternions and 4 quinions. The quire structure follows Gregory's rule (flesh facing flesh, hair facing hair).
The quire number, preserved only in some cases, is placed in the lower right corner of the final leaf of the quire, within a frame of signs.

condition.p: The codex is now disbound; each leaf is housed in a cardboard folder and kept in a safe. The manuscript is generally in good condition, except for some leaves that have suffered from humidity. The ink on the final leaf is heavily faded. One leaf (f. 38) is torn.

layout.p: The text is arranged in a single column of writing, with the exception of the "Genealogy of Jesus" (Luke 3:23–38), which is laid out in two columns.

Ruling: The guide holes for ruling are not visible; the ruling was impressed dry, apparently one bifolium at a time, on the flesh side. The written area includes a single marginal ruling line and is divided into two parts.
The upper part, larger and reserved for the text, measures 130 × 165 mm and is divided into 20 lines, upon which the letters rest, bounded above by an additional ruling line.

The lower part, smaller, begins approximately one centimetre below the last line of the upper system. It consists of 11 evenly spaced parallel lines and has a height of ca. 33–35 mm. This system contains the four Eusebian canon tables on each page.
The proportions of the written area on each page follow the principle of the golden ratio (ca. 210 × 130 mm).

handNote.p: Scribe of the Gospels of Matthew and John. The text is written in scriptio continua in the vertical Gothic script (with <s> of Latin form), set within an actually drawn bilinear system. The hand is highly regular.
Scribe of the Gospels of Luke and Mark. The hand is highly regular, though slightly slenderer than Hand I.

Fifteen marginal glosses are present, also in silver ink and in the vertical script, perhaps added in the same scriptorium in which the manuscript was produced, but apparently by another (single?) hand.

scriptNote.p: Vertical Gothic script with <s> of Latin form, written in scriptio continua within a bilinear system.
A larger module is used to mark the initial letter of a new textual unit, generally corresponding to a new Eusebian section, projected into the outer margin.
To keep the writing within the right margin, smaller-module letters, abbreviations for nasals, and very rarely ligatures (for mu, ht, rþ, þr) may be employed.

decoNote.p: Simplified architectural frames, drawn in silver ink and without painted completion, are present at the foot of the page; they contain the Eusebian canon tables.
Initial letters of new textual units are written in larger module and projected into the outer margin.
The colophon of the Gospel of Mark: aiwaggeljo · þ(ai)rh · m(a)r(ku) · | ustauh · wulþus · þus | weiha · g(u)þ · amen ("The Gospel according to Mark is finished. Glory to you, O holy God. Amen").

item.label: Book titles
item.p: Preserved at the beginnings of the Gospels of Luke and Mark: › aiwaggeljo · þairh · lukan · anastodeiþ › "(the) Gospel according to Luke begins" (f. 118r) and › aiwaggeljo · þairh marku · anastodeiþ › "(the) Gospel according to Mark begins" (f. 57r). Written in silver ink, in a smaller and more compressed module.

item.label: Running titles
item.p: Written every two leaves in the upper central margin on the flesh side, resting on a ruling line. On the verso appears þairh ("according to"), and on the recto the abbreviated accusative form of the evangelist's name.

item.label: Eusebian apparatus
item.p: The text of each Gospel is divided into sequentially numbered sections (355 in Matthew, 233 in Mark, 342 in Luke, and 232 in John). Canon tables are placed in the lower part of each page.

item.label: Paragraph marks
item.p: Thin horizontal stroke, thickened at the ends, with a central sign resembling a dot or a diplé, written in gold ink, placed in the left margin.

item.label: Citation marks
item.p: Quotations from the Old Testament are marked in the left margin with a diplé (>), in silver ink, extending along the entire quotation.

item.label: Punctuation
item.p: The medial point marks minor pauses (commata), and the colon marks major pauses (cola).

item.label: Abbreviations
item.p: Both nasals are abbreviated at line end; nomina sacra for "God", "Lord", "Jesus", and "Christ" are present in contracted form; evangelists' names in running titles are abbreviated.

item.label: Corrections
item.p: Occasional corrections consist of interlinear additions and, in one case, a marginal addition (f. 61v), as well as erasures and rewritings of individual letters; likely contemporary with the text and by the same scribe, written in silver ink.

item.label: Glosses
item.p: Fifteen marginal glosses in silver ink and vertical script, perhaps added in the same scriptorium, apparently by another hand. Framed by reference marks.

binding.p: No traces of the original binding survive. The original outer covering was most probably made of wooden boards, as suggested by the worm damage to the final leaf.
The silver cover bearing the image of Wulfila dates to the 1660s and is now detached.
The codex is now disbound; each leaf is housed in a cardboard folder.

seal.p: The manuscript is written in silver and gold ink. The main body of the text, book titles, running titles, citation marks, section numbers, and Eusebian apparatus are in silver. Gold ink is used for the first three lines of Luke and Mark, the beginning of each Eusebian section, paragraph marks, abbreviations of evangelists' names in canon tables, and other specific elements.

origin.origDate: The codex can plausibly be dated to the first quarter of the sixth century.
origin.origPlace: The manuscript was most likely copied in Ravenna, the capital of the Ostrogothic kingdom and a major cultural centre.
origin.p: The care with which the manuscript was produced and its luxurious character indicate a highly prestigious patronage, identifiable with Theoderic the Great († 526), king of the Ostrogoths, and/or the palatine church.

provenance.p: The history of the Codex Argenteus is known only from the mid-sixteenth century, when its presence at the German monastery of Werden, near Essen, is attested by Georg Cassander and Cornelius Wouters. Nothing is known about when or how the manuscript arrived there.
At the behest of Emperor Rudolf II, the codex passed from Werden to Prague.
The manuscript came into Swedish hands as war booty (1648) and was included among the book treasures of Queen Christina of Sweden.

Donated to Queen Christina's librarian Isaac Vossius, it ended up in the Netherlands, where it was first printed by Vossius's uncle Franciscus Junius (Quattuor […] evangeliorum versiones perantiquae duae, Gotica scilicet et Anglosaxonica, Dordrecht, 1665).

acquisition.p: In 1662 the Swedish count Magnus Gabriel De la Gardie purchased the manuscript and brought it back to Sweden. In 1669 he donated it to the University of Uppsala, where it is still preserved.

provenance.p: The final leaf of the Codex Argenteus (Speyer fragment), containing the end of the Gospel of Mark, came to light in October 1970 in Speyer, during restoration work on the chapel of St Afra. The humanist Philipp Melanchthon handled the leaf in 1518–1519.

recordHist.p: A colour digitalisation, curated by Lars Munkhammar, Magnús Snædal, and David Landau, is available on the website https://www.ub.uu.se/about-the-library/exhibitions/codex-argenteus/.

custodialHist.p: The photographic facsimile of 1927 was prepared by Otto von Friesen and Anders Grape.
